slots.text: Most founders skip validation because they think their idea is different. It never is. The market doesn't care about your clever twist until you prove people actually want the thing.

3 signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They love everything you show them
2. They ask when it's launching instead of how it works
3. They suggest features you'd never build

Find the people who push back.
AI tools are supposed to remove friction but most just move it around. Now instead of doing the task, you're prompt engineering and cleaning up outputs. Same time investment, different headache.
Founders who validate ideas by building full prototypes skip the most important question: would anyone pay for this before it exists.
User interviews are not market research. Stop asking what people want and start watching what they actually do when they think no one's looking.
Workflow automation breaks the moment something changes upstream. You optimize for today's process and lock yourself into yesterday's thinking. The real win is building systems that adapt.
Most founders skip validation because they're afraid their idea isn't original. Here's the thing: if no one else is doing it, that's usually a red flag, not a green one.

Three ways user interviews go wrong:
1. You ask what they want instead of what they do
2. You pitch your solution mid-conversation
3. You talk to people who look like users but aren't actually users

The AI tooling paradox: we have incredible models now, but most founders are still building the same CRUD apps with a ChatGPT wrapper. The real opportunity is using AI to eliminate entire workflows, not just make them slightly faster.

Noticed something: founders who manually do their target workflow for a week before building anything ship products that actually solve real problems. The ones who skip this step build features no one uses.
Removing friction isn't about making things faster. It's about removing the mental overhead of having to think about the thing at all.

Signs you're validating an idea vs validating your ego:
1. You change your approach based on user feedback
2. You're genuinely surprised by what you learn
3. You kill features users don't care about
4. You ask follow-up questions when they say 'yes'
Most founders think user interviews are about validation. They're actually about invalidation. The faster you kill bad assumptions, the faster you find what actually matters.

AI tools that actually save me time:
1. Auto-generating user interview scripts from personas
2. Pulling insights from messy customer feedback
3. Writing first drafts of feature specs

Everything else feels like a solution looking for a problem.

The hardest part about idea validation isn't finding people to talk to. It's admitting when they're telling you your idea sucks. Everyone wants to be polite. You have to read between the lines of 'that's interesting' and 'I could see that being useful.'
Noticed a pattern: founders who obsess over removing one click from their workflow will add three steps to their customer's workflow without thinking twice about it.
User interviews where people say they love your idea are useless. User interviews where people hang up on you teach you everything.

Signs your workflow is too complicated:
1. You need a checklist to use your own product
2. New team members ask 'why do we do it this way'
3. You catch yourself explaining workarounds to users
4. The happy path has six steps
Most founders skip validation because they think they already know their users. Then spend 6 months building something nobody wants.

3 things that kill user interviews:
1. Leading questions that confirm your bias
2. Talking more than listening
3. Not asking about their current workaround
The hardest part of building with AI isn't the tech stack. It's figuring out which parts of your workflow actually need to be automated vs which parts users want control over.
Friction isn't always bad. Users will tolerate 5 extra clicks if it means they understand what's happening. They won't tolerate one black box decision.
Your idea doesn't need to be revolutionary. It needs to solve a real problem better than the spreadsheet they're using now.

Signs you're removing the wrong friction:
1. Usage drops after you 'simplify'
2. Support tickets about lost features
3. Power users start asking for the old version
Most founders think validation means asking "would you use this?" Wrong question. Ask "what did you do the last three times you faced this problem?" Their actual behavior tells the real story.

Why user interviews go sideways:

1. You're pitching instead of listening
2. Leading questions that confirm your bias
3. Talking to people who are too polite to disagree
4. Not digging into their current workarounds

The AI integration trap: everyone's bolting ChatGPT onto their workflow and calling it innovation. But most workflows are broken to begin with. Adding AI to a messy process just makes it messier faster.
Founders who spend months perfecting their landing page before talking to a single user have a 90% chance of building something nobody wants. The correlation is almost mathematical.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes friction is the only thing preventing your users from making expensive mistakes. Remove the right friction, keep the guardrails.

Signs your idea validation is actually working:

1. Users describe their pain without you prompting
2. They ask when they can start paying
3. They introduce you to others with the same problem
4. They're already hacking together solutions
Most founders skip the boring part of validation: actually using their own product daily. You catch friction faster than any user interview ever will.

Three things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions that confirm your bias
2. Talking to people who will never pay
3. Asking what they want instead of watching what they do
The AI wrapper trap is real. Everyone's building the same ChatGPT interface with domain-specific prompts. The value isn't in the AI—it's in the workflow you're actually replacing.
Founders who manually do their product's core workflow for weeks before building anything ship features users actually need. The rest build feature graveyards.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes the steps you want to remove are the ones that make users think twice—which is exactly what they should be doing.

Signs your idea needs more validation:

1. You're explaining the problem to potential users
2. Every demo starts with "imagine if..."
3. You haven't personally felt the pain you're solving
4. Your landing page is all features, no outcomes
Most founders skip validation because they're afraid of hearing 'no.' But 'no' with reasons is infinitely more valuable than 'maybe' without context.

User interviews that actually matter:
1. Ask about their current solution, not your idea
2. Listen for emotion in their voice when describing pain
3. Follow up with 'show me' not 'tell me'
4. End with 'who else has this problem?'

Everyone talks about building with AI but most founders are just adding ChatGPT to their form submissions. The real opportunity is using AI to eliminate entire steps in user workflows, not just make existing steps slightly better.
Founders who talk to 5 users think they need better questions. Founders who talk to 50 users realize they need better listening skills.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes the extra step is what makes people value what they're getting. Remove friction from outcomes, not from commitment.

Signs your idea validation is working:
1. Users interrupt you to ask pricing
2. They introduce you to colleagues unprompted
3. They complain about their current solution getting worse
4. They ask when it'll be ready
